opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's worth pointing out that this isn't actually a new situation. Nobody fully understands the software stack they're running today. If you write a Python script, you don't understand the interpreter line by line, or the operating system, or the firmware on your CPU. We've always relied on layers of abstraction that someone else built and that we trust because they've been tested and they behave predictably within known boundaries.

What's different with AI-generated code is the *nature* of that trust. Traditional abstractions are designed by humans with intent. There's a specification, a mental model somewhere that maps to what the code does, and if something breaks, there's a person who can reason about why. When you have a model generating large amounts of code that nobody has a mental model of, you lose that. You end up with something that passes the tests you thought to write, but you don't really know how it will behave outside of that envelope. And software failures are almost always outside the envelope you anticipated.

So for me, the key question isn't "do I understand every line?" It's "do I have a reliable way to verify behavior, and do I have a model of the system at the right level of abstraction?" If you can specify what you want formally, or at least with very strong tests, and verify that the generated code meets that spec, then not reading every line is fine. That's just delegation. But if your only evidence that it works is that it seemed to work when you tried it, you're accumulating a kind of comprehension debt. It's like technical debt, but worse, because you don't even know where it is.

And I think there's a deeper issue too. Understanding isn't just a tool for debugging. It's how you adapt the system later. If you don't understand the code, you can't evolve it with intent; you can only ask the model to patch it again and hope. Over time, you get a codebase that's essentially a pile of local fixes with no global coherence. That's fine for throwaway scripts, but for anything that needs to live for years, I'd be very careful.

So I'm not against it. I think it's going to be a big part of how software gets built. But the skill that becomes most valuable is not writing code, it's specifying intent precisely and verifying outcomes rigorously. That's where human understanding still has to live.

r001.rationale: The response says nobody fully understands the software stack they run and gives the interpreter, operating system, and CPU firmware as examples of layers beyond any one user's complete understanding.

r002.rationale: It says understanding every line is unnecessary when people have a system model at the right level of abstraction and can specify goals and verify behavior against a spec or strong tests.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that we've been doing this for a long time already. Nobody fully understands the software they run. If you're using a modern operating system, a web browser, a compiler, there are millions of lines of code in there that you have never read and never will. So in some sense, "running code you don't fully understand" is just the normal state of software engineering. We manage it through abstraction, through interfaces, through contracts: I don't need to know how the TCP stack works, I need to know what guarantees it gives me.

What's different with deep learning is that the thing you don't understand is not just large, it's a different kind of object. A neural network is not code in the traditional sense. It's a parametric curve fitted to a dataset. There's no decomposition into parts with legible semantics. You can't read it, you can't reason about it locally, and crucially, you can't write down the contract it satisfies. You can only characterize its behavior statistically, on the distribution you tested it on. The moment you step outside that distribution, the guarantees evaporate, and you typically don't know that you've stepped outside.

So my view is that this is fine, even desirable, for the kinds of problems where that's the appropriate tool: perception, pattern matching, anything where you have lots of data and the cost of an error is low or recoverable. Where it gets dangerous is when people treat these systems as if they were engineered artifacts with reliable properties, and put them in the loop for things where failures are expensive or irreversible. The failure mode isn't that the code is opaque. It's that the opacity gets mistaken for competence.

And then there's a deeper question, which is whether opacity is fundamental or whether it's a property of the current paradigm. I think it's largely the latter. If you build systems that actually synthesize programs, that produce discrete, compositional, verifiable structures, then you get back something you can inspect and reason about, even if the process that produced it was a search you didn't directly control. That's the direction I find much more interesting than just scaling the curve-fitting and hoping interpretability catches up afterward. The goal should be systems that generate understanding, not systems that replace it.

r001.rationale: The response says nobody fully understands the software they run and points to modern systems with millions of lines of code that users never read.

r002.rationale: It says this is manageable through abstractions, interfaces, and contracts: you need to know a component’s guarantees, not how it works internally.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between understanding every line of code and understanding what a system does well enough to trust it. We already use software that no single person understands in its entirety. But we manage that complexity through interfaces, tests, and abstractions. You can reason about a component without having to keep its entire implementation in your head.

The concern is when you lose that ability to reason about the system at all. If you generate a lot of code, and your only evidence that it works is that it appears to work on a few examples, then you have a problem. How do you know what happens in a situation you didn't anticipate? How do you fix it when it breaks?

So I'm comfortable with automating the production of code. But you still need specifications, verification, and some way for a human to understand the relevant behavior. Producing software is not just producing code. It's being able to establish that the code does what you intended.

r001.rationale: It says we already use software that no single person understands in its entirety.

r002.rationale: It accepts that people need not understand every line, as long as specifications are clear and humans can reason about the system’s relevant behavior and verify that it meets the intended behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between understanding how a system was constructed and understanding how it behaves. We already use software that no single person understands in its entirety. But we have ways of breaking it into components, specifying what those components should do, and testing those assumptions.

With machine learning, you can understand every line of the training code and still have a very incomplete understanding of the resulting system. The program you wrote is effectively producing another program, and that second program doesn’t come with a specification or a clear account of its limits.

So I’m comfortable with incomplete understanding when we can bound the consequences of failure and independently verify the outputs. I’m much less comfortable giving such a system broad autonomy in a setting where mistakes are difficult to detect or reverse. The important question is: what evidence do we have that it will behave appropriately outside the situations we’ve tested?

r001.rationale: The response says we already use software that no single person understands in its entirety, which conveys that substantial systems exceed any one engineer’s complete understanding.

r002.rationale: The response accepts incomplete understanding when failure consequences can be bounded and outputs independently verified, but does not clearly state that this depends on understanding the system’s high-level goals and constraints.
